items.title: Reading for pleasure isn’t just passing the time — psychology links it to lower stress and reduced dementia risk
items.summary:
If you’ve ever settled into a chair with a novel, a magazine, or a comic book on a quiet afternoon, you may have felt a mild twinge of guilt. Compared to exercising or catching up with friends, reading purely for fun can look a little too passive—like a pleasant way to kill an hour rather than a habit that meaningfully supports your health.

Yet that quiet pastime may be doing far more behind the scenes than most people realize, especially in later life. And you don’t have to force yourself through dense classics for it to count. Researchers use a surprisingly open definition: anything you choose to read simply because you want to, from paperbacks and nonfiction to digital reads, magazines, comics, and graphic novels.

A quiet buffer for the aging mind 
 Why would an everyday leisure habit matter as the brain gets older? A big part of the explanation comes down to cognitive reserve—the mental buffer that helps a brain keep working smoothly even when aging or injury starts to take a toll. Activities that keep your mind actively engaged are thought to build that reserve over time.

To evaluate how recreational reading fits into that picture, Barbara J. Sahakian of the University of Cambridge and her colleagues pulled together findings from long-term cohort studies, brain-imaging research, and literacy surveys in an editorial synthesis published in Psychological Medicine. Looking at voluntary reading through the lens of preventive psychiatry, they examined how this accessible, low-cost habit might support mental well-being and help protect the aging brain.

items.title: Declining public healthcare access fuels lasting support for populist right parties in England
items.summary:
When local public medical clinics shut down in England, nearby residents report worse healthcare access and become more likely to back right-wing populist parties, according to new research published in American Political Science Review . This shift in voting intentions lasts for several years and tends to be strongest in areas experiencing higher immigration. The findings suggest that everyday breakdowns in government services can fuel anti-establishment sentiment, particularly where political messaging portrays newcomers as competing for scarce public resources.

Populist right parties combine anti-establishment appeals, pitting ordinary citizens against what they cast as a corrupt elite, with nationalist and anti-immigration platforms. Scholars have often traced these parties’ appeal to economic upheaval from globalization or cultural backlash against rising diversity, paying less attention to citizens’ everyday experiences with the state.

Public services such as healthcare, schools, and transit form an unspoken social contract in which citizens pay taxes and obey laws in return for reliable public goods. Even politically disengaged residents notice when their local clinic closes or wait times lengthen, encouraging the view that mainstream leaders are breaking that bargain.

Recent studies have traced how government cutbacks and disappearing local institutions feed into protest voting. In Britain, a 2019 economic study found that people and regions hit hardest by post-2010 welfare cuts became more likely to back the UK Independence Party and vote to leave the European…

items.title: Understanding emotion-focused coping: What decades of psychology research reveal
items.summary:
When life brings a stressful demand that feels bigger than what we can easily handle, psychologists call our mental and behavioral efforts to manage that pressure “coping.” Rather than acting as a fixed habit that never changes, coping is an active process that shifts as stressful situations unfold.

In a landmark 1980 study , psychologists Susan Folkman and Richard Lazarus tracked 100 men and women aged 45 to 64 for an entire year, analyzing 1,332 everyday stressful events. They divided coping into two main jobs: problem-focused coping, which tries to alter or fix the stressful situation itself, and emotion-focused coping, which tries to soothe or regulate the painful feelings sparked by the event.

People almost never rely on just one approach at a time, using both problem-focused and emotion-focused coping together in 98 percent of those 1,332 episodes. As Lazarus later warned in a passage highlighted by Jennifer Austenfeld and Annette Stanton’s 2004 review , treating problem-focused and emotion-focused coping as rigid, separate action boxes or pitting one against the other as the winner misses how real coping works.

Folkman and Lazarus also found that people shifted their coping patterns from one event to the next depending on the setting and on “cognitive appraisal,” a psychology term for how a person evaluates what is at stake and what can be done. Work problems and situations judged changeable pulled toward problem-focused coping, while health concerns and situations judged as having to be accepted pulled toward emotion-focused coping.

items.t: Understanding emotion-focused coping: What decades of psychology research reveal

items.title: Long-term singlehood doesn’t follow a single emotional script — a psychology study of 2,930 adults tracked how solo life unfolds over 11 years
items.summary:
If you’ve been single for a while, there’s a quiet question that tends to surface at weddings, family dinners, or slow Sunday evenings. Does staying unpartnered mean your happiness is slowly ticking downward? 

For decades, everyday culture—and plenty of traditional lifespan psychology—treated finding a partner as a universal milestone for a good life. Under that script, wanting a relationship you haven’t found yet, or feeling underwhelmed by your dating life, can feel like proof that your overall well-being must be suffering. 

Daily life is rarely that tidy. Plenty of people stay single for years, still feel a pull toward partnership or mixed feelings about their sex lives, and yet feel genuinely content with their lives overall. 

Separating romance from the rest of life 
 That split between how you feel about being single and how you feel about your life as a whole sits at the heart of research led by Elaine Hoan, a PhD candidate at the University of Toronto, and her colleagues. In a study published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin , the team analyzed survey data from 2,930 never-married adults in Germany who remained unpartnered across 11 years, spanning emerging, young, and middle adulthood. 

Earlier work on the same dataset blended everyone into a single average curve, making it appear that singles’ happiness gradually declined. Instead, Hoan’s team grouped participants by their distinct long-term patterns across separate measures: overall life satisfaction, satisfaction with being single, sexual satisfaction, and desire for a partner. 

What emerged…
items.t: Long-term singlehood doesn’t follow a single emotional script — a psychology study of 2,930 adults tracked how solo life unfolds over 11 years

items.title: How education and marriage patterns shape household wealth in urban China
items.summary:
In urban China, married couples where both partners hold college degrees accumulate the highest levels of household wealth, while couples without college degrees face persistent financial disadvantages. A large study published in the Journal of Marriage and Family also found that households benefit financially when both spouses work, though this advantage diminishes for the wealthiest families. These patterns highlight how marriage and education combine to shape economic inequality in a rapidly changing society.

Private wealth has emerged as a primary measure of financial security and social status in China following economic reforms that began in the late 1970s. Before these reforms, the state controlled most assets. Today, households are largely responsible for securing their own housing, education, and retirement funds. In the modern Chinese economy, home equity is a major component of wealth for families.

Yu Wang, a researcher at Duke Kunshan University, and Lisa A. Keister, a sociologist at Duke University, conducted the large study to understand how family formation influences asset accumulation. They focused on educational assortative mating, a term describing the tendency for people to marry partners with similar educational backgrounds. The researchers wanted to see how combining different levels of education within a marriage might relate to a family’s overall net worth. They also looked at whether having both partners in the workforce altered these financial outcomes.

To explore these dynamics, Wang and Keister analyzed data from the 2019 China Household…
items.t: How education and marriage patterns shape household wealth in urban China

items.title: Popular “smart drug” Ritalin unexpectedly curbs dishonesty in healthy adults
items.summary:
Healthy adults who take a single dose of the prescription stimulant methylphenidate, commonly sold as Ritalin, tend to cheat less for money than those given an inactive placebo, according to new research published in Psychopharmacology . Comparing methylphenidate against both a placebo and a non-stimulant medication, the researchers found evidence that this drop in dishonesty was not a byproduct of sharper focus, mood shifts, or expectations about the pill. A follow-up national survey indicated that everyday Americans, including people who use prescription stimulants to boost productivity, generally do not anticipate this behavioral side effect.

Methylphenidate is a prescription central nervous system stimulant primarily used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Physically, it blocks nerve cells in the brain from reabsorbing dopamine and norepinephrine, two chemical messengers, known as neurotransmitters, that are involved in concentration, motivation, and reward, leaving higher amounts active between neurons.

Growing numbers of students, financial workers, academics, and military personnel without ADHD take such medications hoping to gain a mental edge. In a global survey cited by the authors, 14% of respondents reported taking drugs like methylphenidate or atomoxetine to boost cognitive performance in the past year, up from 5% in 2015. That trend aligns with an earlier study comparing off-prescription smart-drug users with non-users , which indicated that healthy takers use these substances to optimize normal cognitive speed rather than to offset…
items.t: Popular “smart drug” Ritalin unexpectedly curbs dishonesty in healthy adults

items.title: New psychiatry review finds little consensus on which conditions count as “neurodivergent”
items.summary:
A comprehensive review of mental health research published in JAMA Psychiatry indicates that scientists use the terms “neurodiversity” and “neurodivergent” inconsistently, applying them to two dozen distinct clinical categories or leaving out medical criteria altogether. Most of the reviewed studies relied on participants’ self-identification or self-reported diagnoses rather than clinical records, frequently grouping varied conditions such as autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and anxiety under a single umbrella. The authors suggest that although these terms help capture personal identity and lived experience, substituting broad labels for specific diagnoses in clinical research may obscure distinct support needs and treatment responses.

Developed by autistic activists in the mid-1990s, the concept of neurodiversity carries three related meanings today. As a descriptive term, neurodiversity refers to the natural variation in how human brains develop, think, and process information across an entire group or population. Because variety is a property of a group rather than a single person, an individual cannot technically be “neurodiverse”; instead, someone whose cognitive functioning differs from conventional social norms is described as “neurodivergent,” whereas someone within typical social expectations is considered “neurotypical.”

Beyond describing brain differences, neurodiversity also functions as a theoretical framework and a social rights movement. The framework approaches cognitive differences as natural human variations rather than medical deficits, emphasizing personal…
items.t: New psychiatry review finds little consensus on which conditions count as “neurodivergent”

items.title: Frequent sleepwalking and sleep terrors at age 4 are linked to more behavioral problems a year later
items.summary:
A longitudinal study in Canada found that children who had more frequent sleepwalking and sleep terror episodes at 4 years of age tended to have more emotional (internalizing) and behavioral (externalizing) problems at that age. They also tended to have more behavioral problems a year later, at age 5. The paper was published in the Journal of Sleep Research .

Sleep problems are common during childhood, and sleepwalking and sleep terrors are two particularly frequent disturbances, collectively known as disorders of arousal. These episodes occur when children partially awaken from non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. During them, children may sit up, get out of bed and walk around while still asleep, or scream, cry, and appear terrified.

Although these episodes usually disappear naturally as children grow older, they can persist into adulthood in some individuals. They may also be associated with poor sleep quality and mental health difficulties. Previous studies have suggested that children experiencing disorders of arousal are more likely to exhibit emotional and behavioral problems, including anxiety, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and psychotic symptoms. However, research findings have been inconsistent, with some studies identifying associations and others finding little or no relationship between these sleep disturbances and psychological difficulties.

One important limitation of previous research is that many studies have relied on clinical samples or cross-sectional designs. This makes it difficult to determine whether their findings…
items.t: Frequent sleepwalking and sleep terrors at age 4 are linked to more behavioral problems a year later

items.title: When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery
items.summary:
The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks. 

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the Vancouver Art Gallery , and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend PaRx , Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access.

Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.…
items.t: When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery

items.title: Childhood emotional abuse linked to adult mental health struggles more strongly than physical or sexual abuse
items.summary:
Childhood emotional abuse often receives less public and clinical attention than physical or sexual mistreatment, yet a large analysis published in Psychological Bulletin indicates its connection to adult mental health difficulties is just as strong, and frequently stronger.

Synthesizing data from 113,673 adults across 104 studies, researchers found that early emotional mistreatment showed a stronger statistical relationship with conditions such as depression, anxiety, and personality disorders than physical or sexual abuse. The findings challenge the common assumption that nonphysical mistreatment is a less harmful form of childhood adversity.

Why childhood emotional abuse often goes unrecognized 
 Childhood emotional abuse, sometimes called psychological abuse, consists of nonaccidental verbal or symbolic actions by a parent or caregiver that convey to a child that they are worthless, unloved, flawed, unwanted, or unsafe. Specific behaviors include persistent criticism, insults, humiliation, threats of abandonment, repeated blaming, or isolating a child from normal social interactions. Unlike emotional neglect, which involves passive failures to provide affection and support, emotional abuse involves active, hostile behaviors directed at the child.

Physical abuse involves nonaccidental physical force that causes or risks bodily injury, regardless of whether a caregiver intended to cause harm, while sexual abuse involves imposing sexual interactions on a child. Because emotional abuse leaves no physical marks and can resemble ordinary family conflict or strict…
items.t: Childhood emotional abuse linked to adult mental health struggles more strongly than physical or sexual abuse

items.title: Machine-learning models can detect elevated psychopathy and sadism from reactions to funny pictures
items.summary:
The way people react to internet memes, cartoons, and absurd pictures may carry subtle clues about socially aversive aspects of their personality. A new study published in Journal of Individual Differences indicates that machine-learning models analyzing how funny and cruel people find visual jokes can identify elevated levels of psychopathy and everyday sadism, and to a lesser degree narcissism, though not Machiavellianism.

The findings suggest that patterns in humor appreciation could eventually offer researchers an indirect way to study dark personality traits without relying entirely on people’s willingness to report their own flaws.

Why humor offers an indirect window into dark personality traits 
 Psychologists use the term Dark Tetrad to describe a cluster of four overlapping yet distinct socially aversive personality traits: Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy, and everyday sadism. Machiavellianism involves strategic manipulation and a cynical view of human nature, while narcissism centers on grandiosity, entitlement, and a strong desire for admiration. Psychopathy is marked by impulsivity, emotional coldness, and low empathy, whereas everyday sadism refers to taking pleasure from watching or causing others’ discomfort in daily life.

Higher levels of these four traits have been linked to harmful outcomes ranging from workplace misconduct to online harassment and relationship aggression. Even so, measuring them accurately remains a persistent challenge in psychology.

items.t: Machine-learning models can detect elevated psychopathy and sadism from reactions to funny pictures

items.title: Study suggests cognitive skills shape how young children learn new words from screen versus paper books
items.summary:
Young children appear to learn new words from a storybook read aloud by a caregiver about equally well on average whether the book is printed on paper or displayed on a tablet, according to new research published in the Journal of Experimental Child Psychology . Beneath that overall tie, how well preschoolers recognized newly introduced words from a screen depended on their individual attention, memory, and self-control skills. Children who scored higher on these skills fared better on word comprehension when reading on an iPad, whereas peers with less developed skills fared better with a paper book.

Shared book reading, the everyday practice in which an adult and child sit together to read and talk through a book aloud, is an important driver of early vocabulary growth. Picture books expose children to rarer, more varied words than everyday conversation, and caregivers naturally pause to point at illustrations and explain unfamiliar terms, a form of supportive guidance known as scaffolding. Consistent with this role, a study of preschool children indicated that trading general screen time for parent-child reading was tied to stronger language and social-emotional skills, whereas replacing shared reading with solo screen use, even educational content, was linked to lower developmental scores.

As tablets have become household staples, shared reading now happens on screens as well as on paper. Paper books generally serve a single purpose, whereas tablets are multipurpose touchscreens associated with videos and games. Observational studies suggest that reading together on…
items.t: Study suggests cognitive skills shape how young children learn new words from screen versus paper books

items.title: Problematic smartphone use predicts a rebound in attention issues during late adolescence
items.summary:
Adolescents who struggle to control their smartphone use tend to experience higher levels of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder-like symptoms as they grow older. A large new study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders found that these symptoms generally decline in early adolescence but bounce back in later teenage years. The researchers observed that problematic smartphone use consistently predicted worse symptom severity over time.

Adolescence marks a period of intense brain development where different neural systems mature at varying rates. The brain regions responsible for processing rewards and emotions often develop earlier than the prefrontal areas responsible for self-control and regulation. This temporary imbalance can make teenagers particularly susceptible to attention difficulties, impulsive behaviors, and a desire for immediate gratification.

While full clinical diagnoses of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder are typically made in childhood, many youths exhibit related traits on a continuous spectrum. These traits include hyperactivity, inattention, and impulsivity that fluctuate naturally as a child grows. The way these symptoms express themselves can change depending on a teenager’s changing environment and developmental stage.

At the same time, teenagers today grow up in environments saturated with digital technology. Problematic smartphone use occurs when individuals struggle to control their screen time. They feel compelled to use their devices to the point that it interferes with their daily functioning. This is not simply…
items.t: Problematic smartphone use predicts a rebound in attention issues during late adolescence

items.title: Cynical hostility and lack of assertiveness both predict depression decades later
items.summary:
A 23-year study of Swedish twins suggests that cynical hostility and difficulty standing up for oneself are both linked to worse depressive symptoms later in life, even after accounting for shared genetics. Published in Psychological Medicine , the research indicates that hostile attitudes tend to shrink a person’s circle of friends over time, which in turn relates to greater depression severity. At the same time, a proposed chain reaction from unassertiveness to growing hostility was not statistically significant between identical twins, suggesting that overlapping genetic traits may connect those two tendencies.

Lack of assertiveness refers to an ongoing difficulty expressing one’s own needs, boundaries, or preferences, such as struggling to refuse unwanted requests and holding back frustration rather than speaking constructively. Psychologists view this interpersonal pattern as a vulnerability for depression, a mood condition marked by persistent sadness, loss of interest, and impaired daily functioning. Early clinical work, including a 1980 clinical trial , found that training people to communicate more assertively helped relieve depressive symptoms.

When unexpressed needs pile up and everyday conflicts go unresolved, unassertiveness may foster resentment-based hostility. This form of hostility describes a persistent distrust of others, accompanied by lingering anger and a cynical belief that most people are dishonest, selfish, or malicious. Hostile attitudes consistently predict worse mood outcomes; for example, a 2010 longitudinal study of 296 older adults found…
items.t: Cynical hostility and lack of assertiveness both predict depression decades later

items.title: Psychologists pooled 80 years of data to answer a basic question about what aging does to our personalities
items.summary:
As people move from childhood into old age, their personalities tend to mature on average, yet a large new analysis indicates that the overall spread of personality differences across the population stays remarkably constant. Combining data from nearly 400,000 individuals tracked over time, the research published in Psychological Bulletin suggests that people neither grow more alike nor drift further apart in their core traits as they get older.

Because individual differences remain just as wide in late adulthood as in youth, personality traits retain their power to help explain why people differ in health, relationships, and work outcomes throughout life.

Why psychologists study the spread of personality differences 
 Personality traits are enduring patterns in how people think, feel, and behave across everyday situations. Psychologists commonly group these tendencies into the Big Five traits: openness to experience (curiosity and imagination), conscientiousness (organization and self-discipline), extraversion (sociability and energy), agreeableness (warmth and cooperativeness), and neuroticism (moodiness and emotional vulnerability).

Beyond measuring a group’s average score on each trait, researchers can examine a trait’s variance, a statistical measure of how widely individuals in a population differ from one another. Shrinking variance over time would mean people’s personalities are converging toward a common mold, whereas growing variance would mean individual differences become more pronounced with age.

Previous developmental studies have mostly tracked two other…
items.t: Psychologists pooled 80 years of data to answer a basic question about what aging does to our personalities

items.title: What Happens When Elders Share Their Stories
items.summary:
When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories. 

The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories . The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third. 

What is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

Fostering connections and reflection 

Storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. Uri Hasson and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy. 

The more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes…
items.t: What Happens When Elders Share Their Stories

items.title: Better sexual mentalizing is linked to better sexual function and more sex over time
items.summary:
A study of German-speaking adults surveyed twice, about four months apart, found that people with better sexual mentalizing abilities (i.e., those better able to understand their own and others’ thoughts, feelings, and desires in sexual situations) tended to report better sexual function and more partnered sex four months later. The reverse was also the case. Sexual mentalizing did not predict later sexual satisfaction, but greater sexual satisfaction predicted better sexual mentalizing. The paper was published in the Journal of Sex Research .

Mentalizing is the ability to recognize and understand the thoughts, feelings, desires, and intentions that influence one’s own and other people’s behavior. This ability is believed to develop during early childhood through interactions with caregivers who help infants recognize, interpret, and regulate their emotional experiences. However, researchers have proposed that sexual feelings and bodily experiences may follow a different developmental trajectory because caregivers often respond to children’s emerging sexuality with discomfort, embarrassment, or avoidance.

As a result, sexual experiences may remain less integrated into an individual’s understanding of themselves until adolescence or adulthood, when supportive intimate relationships may help them develop a clearer understanding of their sexual feelings and desires. The ability to recognize, interpret, and regulate one’s own and others’ sexual feelings, desires, and experiences is known as sexual mentalizing and is considered distinct from general mentalizing.

items.title: Scientists analyzed over 3,700 daily reports to see how personal traits and real-world events relate to your dreams
items.summary:
New research published in Communications Psychology indicates that dream content follows measurable patterns shaped by both enduring personal traits and major real-world events. Analyzing thousands of daily dream and waking reports collected over four years, scientists found that characteristics such as a tendency to let the mind wander, attitudes toward dreaming, and perceived sleep quality were associated with distinct features of dream narratives. The findings also suggest that large-scale stressors like the COVID-19 lockdown were tied to temporary shifts in dream themes and emotional intensity that gradually faded over the following years.

Dreams are conscious experiences made up of internally generated images, sensations, emotions, and unfolding scenarios that occur during sleep while the brain is partly disconnected from outside sensory input. Rather than serving as literal replays of daily routines, dreams tend to weave fragments of waking concerns and mental habits into altered narratives.

For example, a 2015 study of adults reporting their most recent dreams found that people who habitually try to push away unwanted thoughts during the day tended to dream more about their waking-life emotions. Similarly, an earlier study of work- and hobby-related dreams indicated that greater involvement in hobbies was linked to more frequent hobby-themed dreams, which tended to be more positive in tone than work-related or general dreams. In that same study, higher job stress was associated with more frequent work-related dreams.

items.title: LSD may counter some aging-related brain changes, rodent and cell experiments suggest
items.summary:
Treatment with the classic psychedelic lysergic acid diethylamide, better known as LSD, triggers patterns of gene activity in rodent brains that run counter to the molecular shifts seen during human brain aging and dementia, according to new research published in Aging Cell . In accompanying experiments on mouse brain cells grown in laboratory dishes, short-term exposure to LSD also blunted structural, molecular, and gene-activity disruptions caused by toxic protein clumps linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

Together, the findings offer a molecular starting point for studying whether psychedelic-inspired compounds might support aging brain cells, though whether these effects improve memory or slow decline in living patients remains untested.

Lysergic acid diethylamide is a synthetic psychedelic compound that alters perception, mood, and cognition primarily by binding to and activating specific chemical docking sites on brain cells called serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. Beyond its mind-altering effects, LSD belongs to a group of substances that stimulate neuroplasticity, which is the brain’s physical ability to sprout new nerve branches and remodel the microscopic junctions, known as synapses, where neurons pass signals to one another.

During normal aging, and far more severely in neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer’s disease, those synaptic connections gradually weaken and shrink while nearby support cells become chronically reactive. These changes hit especially hard in the prefrontal cortex, the brain region located right behind the forehead that coordinates planning,…
items.t: LSD may counter some aging-related brain changes, rodent and cell experiments suggest

items.title: Getting news on gaming platforms like Discord and Twitch is linked to more radical political views
items.summary:
Young Europeans who get their news from gaming platforms like Discord, Steam, or Twitch tend to hold stronger radical political views than peers who rely on social media or traditional news, according to research published in Political Psychology .

A similar pattern appeared among youth who get news through private messaging apps like Telegram and WhatsApp. Simply playing video games or using these spaces for everyday socializing, however, was not linked to higher radical beliefs.

Why closed online spaces draw scrutiny 
 Online political talk has increasingly moved from public feeds like Facebook and X into closed spaces, including private messaging apps and gaming-adjacent platforms where players coordinate matches, join private servers, and watch livestreamers. Researchers studying youth extremism are examining how getting news in these spaces relates to radical belief dispositions, a cluster of attitudes spanning conspiracy thinking, authoritarianism, prejudice against minority groups, traditional masculinity, and openness to political violence.

Earlier work has documented how extremist actors target online leisure communities. In a 2024 systematic review of research on right-wing extremism in video games , scholars summarized evidence indicating that far-right groups use hate speech and ideological themes in gaming spaces as an on-ramp to recruit disillusioned players. Meanwhile, a 2022 series of three studies found that players whose personal identities fuse tightly with gamer culture tend to endorse more racism, sexism, and extreme behavior, especially when lonely…
items.t: Getting news on gaming platforms like Discord and Twitch is linked to more radical political views

items.title: Disadvantaged students with a growth mindset are more likely to beat the odds, especially when their peers share it
items.summary:
An analysis of data from more than 600,000 15-year-olds in 79 countries found that socioeconomically disadvantaged students with a growth mindset were more likely to be academically resilient, meaning they reached solid levels of proficiency in reading, math, and science despite their backgrounds. Resilience was most common among students with a growth mindset who also attended schools where their peers tended to hold growth mindsets. The paper was published in npj Science of Learning .

Students from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds tend to face substantial obstacles to academic success. Yet some manage to perform well despite these challenges, an ability known as academic resilience. Researchers have identified various individual and environmental factors that potentially contribute to academic resilience, including students’ confidence, engagement, and academic expectations, as well as a safe and orderly school environment and good teaching.

One potentially important factor is a growth mindset, the belief that intelligence and abilities can be developed through effort and effective learning strategies, rather than being fixed and unchangeable. Students with a growth mindset tend to demonstrate greater perseverance, more adaptive responses to failure, and a stronger willingness to embrace challenges. However, previous research has produced mixed findings about its relationship with academic achievement among disadvantaged students.

Recent research also suggests that the benefits of a growth mindset may depend on the social environment, particularly the…
items.t: Disadvantaged students with a growth mindset are more likely to beat the odds, especially when their peers share it

items.title: Traits that make someone seem more intellectual can also make them seem less liberal, study suggests
items.summary:
People’s impressions of how politically liberal and how intellectual another person is do not behave like two expressions of a single broad personality trait, according to new experimental research published in Journal of Research in Personality . When participants evaluated fictional individuals from brief personality profiles, descriptions that boosted perceived intellect tended to lower perceived liberalism. The findings suggest that combining political attitudes and intellectual curiosity into one broad “openness to experience” score may obscure distinct underlying dimensions in how people judge others.

In psychology, personality is commonly organized around the Big Five model, which groups traits into five broad domains: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness to experience. Openness to experience refers to a person’s tendency to engage with new ideas, art, emotions, and unconventional values.

Widely used personality questionnaires calculate a single overall openness score by adding together six narrower sub-traits, called facets. Two of those facets are intellect, which captures an interest in abstract or philosophical ideas, and liberalism, which reflects progressive political views and a willingness to question traditional rules or authority.

Psychologists have debated whether these varied facets belong on a single psychological spectrum. In a 2007 study , researchers identified two distinct aspects within openness: an intellect aspect centered on reasoning and abstract thought, and an openness aspect centered on aesthetics,…
items.t: Traits that make someone seem more intellectual can also make them seem less liberal, study suggests

items.title: An age gap isn’t always a problem, partner abuse is | Letters
items.summary:
Readers respond to articles on relationships and the age of consent

Regarding Polly Hudson’s article (At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now, 15 November), I met and lived with a 35-year-old man when I was 17. It is obvious now that the relationship was coercively controlling. A divorced father, he had a need to control every aspect of my life, so no makeup, no northern accent, no fatty food (I became anorexic), no scent, no staying out, no heels, no clothes he didn’t like.

I learned that he had done it all before, pursuing schoolgirls. I tried to break free multiple times, only to find that he had phoned my new partner, or read my diary so he could block my plans. This is about having control, it is not just a sexual preference.

Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away.

“It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.”
